stories.headline: Nepal Flash Flood LIVE Updates: Damage May Cost Up To $5 Billion To Rebuild, Says Minister
stories.title: Nepal Flash Flood LIVE Updates: Damage May Cost Up To $5 Billion To Rebuild, Says Minister
stories.summary: Nepal Flash Flood LIVE Updates: A glacier collapse led to a sudden massive flood in the Bhote Koshi River
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

opening: Nepal Flash Flood LIVE Updates: A glacier collapse led to a sudden massive flood in the Bhote Koshi River.
Nepal flash floods has killed hundreds, while thousands are missing.
body: Kathmandu, Aug 29: The death toll from flash floods in central Nepal rose to 675 on Saturday, with more bodies being recovered on Saturday even as more than 2,400 people still remained missing following the disaster.
Bodies were recovered from all eight affected districts as search and rescue operations continued on war footing, Nepal police said.

An ice-rock avalanche following a glacial collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border sent a torrent of water, mud and debris downstream wiping out towns and villages, damaging crucial infrastructure and washing away hydropower stations through central Nepal on Wednesday.
So far, 675 bodies of the Bhote Koshi flood victims have been recovered from eight districts, according to a statement by Nepal.
Police.
The rescuers have recovered 246 bodies from Chitawan, 165 from Nawalparasi East, 63 from Nawalparasi West and 57 from Gorkha, it said.
Similarly, 45 bodies were recovered from Dhading district, 51 from Nuwakot, 35 from Tanahu and 13 from Rasuwa district.
More than 2,400 people remained missing as of Saturday.

Nearly 2,500 people, including 163 foreigners, were evacuated as rescue teams led by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) raced against time amid on-and-off rainfall in the flood-affected regions.
More than 11,000 security personnel, including over 5,000 Nepal Army personnel, have been mobilised for search and rescue operations.
The NDRRMA, in a statement, urged people not to fly drones in the flood affected area, where search and rescue operations are being carried out.

“Our attention has been drawn that there are reports about flying drone by some individuals and organisations without the permission from the local administration at a time when rescue and relief works are in progress,” it said.
The Authority warned of legal action if the law is breached.

stories.title: Flood scare in MP: IAF helicopters, SDRF teams deployed as Mandakini river overflows
stories.summary: Indian Air Force helicopters were deployed to rescue stranded people in Chitrakoot. Torrential rains caused the Mandakini river to overflow, flooding large parts of the town. Three State Disaster Response Force teams were also engaged in shifting people to safer places. A dam breach in Uttar Pradesh worsened the situation, while relief shelters were prepared. The water level in the Mandakini had started receding Saturday night after rainfall paused.

stories.headline: Nepal seeks to import power earlier from India after flood devastation, asks for approvals
stories.title: Nepal seeks to import power earlier from India after flood devastation, asks for approvals
stories.summary: While the Himalayan country usually imports electricity from India during the winter months, it has now asked that the required approvals for sending power be processed in September itself
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: In the wake of the devastating flash flood that severely impacted Nepal’s power infrastructure, Kathmandu has asked India to give the requisite approvals for the transmission of electricity to Nepal earlier than usual, senior officials in the Union Power Ministry said on Saturday (August 29, 2026).
“Nepal has asked that India advance import approvals, starting from September this year, in view of the generation deficits caused by this disaster.
The concerned authorities are processing the requests,” an official said.
According to officials, India is willing to provide any additional power that Nepal may need.
Nepal usually imports electricity from India during the winter months, starting around October, as power generation is typically low in the Himalayan country during the freezing winter months.
Conversely, the country exports its excess hydropower to India during the summer.
According to official data, India imported 3,299 million units (MUs) of power from Nepal in fiscal year 2025-26 and exported 1,451 MUs to it.
Transmission of electricity across India’s borders requires mandatory clearances from the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), among others.
According to an internal assessment, Nepal’s electricity generation capacity has declined by about 550 megawatts because of the infrastructural damage induced by the flood.
Officials said that this resulted in the cross-border power flow to India reducing by approximately 400 MW from earlier peaks of 950 MW to 1,000 MW.
However, the officials assured that India was not foreseeing any requirement to make alternative arrangements to compensate for the shortfall.

“We do not foresee any requirement for exceptional emergency procurement or alternative arrangement to balance domestic demand,” an official said, adding, “India’s vast national grid capacity and robust generation reserve margins are capable of absorbing a temporary shortfall of 400 MW seamlessly without disrupting grid stability or retail supply."

stories.headline: Is Kashmir going Nepal way? Himalayan extremes set alarm bells ringing
stories.title: Is Kashmir going Nepal way? Himalayan extremes set alarm bells ringing
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 29: The devastation in Nepal has sent a chilling warning across Jammu and Kashmir: when a warming climate meets fragile mountain terrain and unchecked human intervention, an extreme weather event can rapidly turn into a catastrophe. For J&K, the question is no longer whether climate change is altering the Himalayan environment. It is whether the Valley is adequately prepared for the increasingly erratic and intense weather events being witnessed across the region. Nepal recently witnessed a devastating flash flood in the Lhende Khola area near the Nepal-Tibet border after an ice-and-rock avalanche entered the river system. The torrent swept away homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure, leaving a trail of destruction and triggering a major rescue operation. The disaster has once again drawn attention to the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities to glacial, geological and weather-related hazards. Kashmir, meanwhile, has been experiencing its own alarming pattern. J&K has witnessed 40 cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides this summer, with incidents reported from Kishtwar, Doda, Ramban, Pahalgam, Shopian, Kulgam, Bandipora and Kupwara. In several cases, streams that normally remain relatively calm have transformed into torrents within minutes, damaging roads, bridges, homes and agricultural land. Climate expert Dr Tauseef Ahmad Bhat said the developments in Nepal should be viewed as a warning for the entire Himalayan region. “Kashmir should not wait for a Nepal-like catastrophe to understand the seriousness of what is happening in the Himalayas. We are witnessing increasing climate volatility, where prolonged dry periods can be followed by short-duration, extremely intense rainfall. In mountainous terrain, even a few minutes of extreme precipitation can trigger flash floods, landslides and debris flows,” Bhat said. He said the concern was not simply about whether Kashmir receives more or less rainfall. “The bigger concern is the changing character of rainfall and the increasing intensity of extreme events. A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, while warming can also contribute to instability of snow, ice and mountain slopes. Kashmir needs to prepare for compound disasters rather than treating every cloudburst as an isolated incident,” he said. Senior environmentalist Dr Tanveer Ahmad Khan said Kashmir’s vulnerability was being compounded by human pressure on an already fragile ecosystem. “Nepal is a warning, not merely a tragedy happening in another Himalayan country. Kashmir shares many of the same vulnerabilities—steep slopes, fragile geology, changing climate and increasing pressure from construction and infrastructure development. If drainage channels, river buffers, wetlands and unstable slopes continue to be disturbed, the impact of extreme weather will become much more severe,” Khan said. He said development planning had to take future climate risks into account. “We cannot continue to build as if the climate of the past is going to remain unchanged. Roads, hydropower projects, tourism infrastructure and settlements in mountain areas must be planned according to future climate risks. Every blocked natural drainage channel and every disturbed vulnerable slope reduces our margin of safety,” Khan added. The Nepal disaster has also underlined how quickly a single extreme event can cripple mountain infrastructure. Roads, bridges and power installations can be destroyed simultaneously, cutting off entire communities and making rescue operations far more difficult. For Kashmir, where highways, hydropower projects, tourism infrastructure and settlements are steadily expanding into mountain areas, experts say the lesson is particularly relevant. Afreen Khurshid, PhD research scholar at the University of Kashmir, said the focus must shift from responding to disasters to anticipating them. “The biggest lesson from Nepal is that vulnerability is created long before a disaster actually occurs. Climate change may intensify the hazard, but exposure and poor planning determine how devastating the final impact becomes. Kashmir urgently needs detailed hazard mapping of slopes, streams, flood channels and settlements, particularly in rapidly developing mountain areas,” she said. Khurshid stressed that early-warning systems must reach vulnerable communities on the ground. “An early warning is useful only when it reaches the last person living near a stream, a shepherd in the upper reaches, a tourist, a pilgrim or a person travelling through a vulnerable mountain corridor. Community preparedness, clearly identified evacuation routes and local response mechanisms can make the difference between an extreme weather event and a mass-casualty disaster,” she said.

stories.headline: Judiciary proactively responded to emerging fraudulent schemes like digital arrest: CJI
stories.title: Judiciary proactively responded to emerging fraudulent schemes like digital arrest: CJI
stories.summary: This exemplifies a broader pattern: an Indian Judiciary that proactively responds to emerging fraudulent schemes, rather than waiting for Parliament to address them, says Chief Justice of India Surya Kant
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in summary weight 25.2
event term: 'chief justice of india' in summary weight 27.6
article_sentences: In his closing address at the 43rd International Symposium on Economic Crime in London, the CJI said the Supreme Court had recently taken suo motu cognisance of the "digital arrest" scam, in which fraudsters impersonate police officers, judicial officials, or bureaucrats over video calls to dupe citizens.

"In response, the court has directed the Union and the States to evaluate the extent of this problem and has called for the establishment of a distinct offence, with penalties proportionate to the harm inflicted," he said.
"This exemplifies a broader pattern: an Indian Judiciary that proactively responds to emerging fraudulent schemes, rather than waiting for Parliament to address them," the CJI said.

He said when one looks at India's modern response to economic crime, it is best understood not as a single statute but as a layered architecture, built deliberately over successive decades, in which legislation, institutions and judicial doctrine are each made to do distinct work.
The CJI referred to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018.
"I must note that these are not infallible mechanisms.

Numerous individuals have alleged misuse of the PMLA process by investigating authorities, including claims of arrests made without articulated reasons, and of custody extended beyond what the existing facts appear to justify.
In each such instance, the judiciary has intervened to rectify the situation," he said.
Justice Kant referred to the apex court's verdict holding that grounds for arrest must be provided to the accused in writing, rather than merely read aloud.

"Furthermore, in Arvind Kejriwal versus Central Bureau of Investigation, a decision I had the opportunity to author, the court upheld the legality of the arrest but nonetheless granted bail, based on the principle that prolonged pre-trial detention should not be transformed into punishment under a different guise," he said.

The CJI said what had remained consistent through the decades, despite legal and technological developments, was the apex court's insistence that due process, proportionality and the presumption of innocence remain the guiding principles of its jurisprudence.

Referring to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the CJI said it runs alongside criminal proceedings and the Indian justice delivery system has grown increasingly comfortable authorising parallel civil recovery even where a criminal trial remains protracted.

stories.headline: Power Tariff Hike: Omar Government Adds to the Burden of the People of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.title: Power Tariff Hike: Omar Government Adds to the Burden of the People of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.summary: ADV SUNIL SETHI The decision to increase electricity tariffs in Jammu & Kashmir at a time when ordinary families are already struggling with the rising cost of living is deeply disappointing. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question of political accountability: what happened to the promises made to the people before the Assembly elections? The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission has approved an average tariff increase of 6.83 per cent, applicable from September 1, 2026. For metered domestic consumers, the rate for consumption up to 200 units has increased from ₹2.30 to ₹2.45 per unit; for 201–400 units, from ₹4.00 to ₹4.20; and above 400 units, from ₹4.35 to ₹4.60 per unit. These figures may appear small when viewed from the comfort of government offices. For an ordinary household, however, every additional financial burden matters. From Promise of Relief to Reality of Higher Bills The National Conference went before the electorate promising 200 units of free electricity. That promise naturally created expectations among families that desperately needed relief. Today, instead of experiencing the promised relief, consumers are confronting increased tariffs. The government may argue that its promise of free electricity and the general electricity tariff are technically separate matters. But politics cannot be reduced to technical explanations. The real question is what an ordinary voter understood when promises of cheaper or free electricity were made. People vote on the basis of promises and the reasonable expectations created by those promises. If financial constraints, distribution losses and the cost of purchasing electricity were realities after the election, they were realities before the election as well. Governments cannot discover economic realities only after obtaining the mandate of the people. Kashmir's Winter Cannot Be Viewed Through Ordinary Consumption Calculations The impact of electricity prices assumes an even greater significance in the Kashmir Valley. For people sitting outside Kashmir, electricity may be regarded primarily as a source of lighting and running household appliances. During Kashmir's severe winter, electricity is intimately connected with survival, warmth and basic human comfort. Temperatures fall below freezing in many areas. Water pipes freeze. Snowfall disrupts normal life. Families depend increasingly upon electric heaters, boilers, geysers, heating blankets and other appliances. The elderly, children and economically weaker families suffer the most. This means that electricity consumption during the harsh winter months cannot simply be treated as discretionary consumption. A Kashmiri family using additional electricity to keep its children or elderly parents warm is not indulging in luxury. It is responding to climatic necessity. And the timing is particularly unfortunate. The revised tariff becomes applicable from September 1 and will remain applicable through the approaching winter until March 31, 2027. The government should therefore ask itself a simple question: Is the period immediately preceding the harsh Kashmir winter the appropriate time to make electricity more expensive for households? Don't Make Consumers Pay for Inefficiency There is undoubtedly a financial problem in the electricity sector. Power has a cost. Distribution companies require revenue, and transmission and distribution losses have historically presented a serious challenge. But the solution cannot perpetually be to transfer the consequences of inefficiency onto honest consumers. The first responsibility of government should be to reduce losses, improve billing and collection, prevent electricity theft, modernise infrastructure and improve the efficiency of distribution companies. A family that pays its electricity bill regularly should not become the easiest source for balancing the books. Before asking consumers to pay more, the government must demonstrate what measurable reduction it has achieved in distribution losses and what administrative reforms it has undertaken to bring down costs. Efficiency must come before additional burden. The Government's Defence Does Not Answer the Political Question Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has defended the increase by arguing that the government never promised that electricity tariffs would remain static and that power continues to be substantially subsidised. That may constitute an administrative defence. It does not answer the political question. The issue is not whether electricity continues to receive subsidy. The issue is whether the government is moving towards the relief that was promised to the electorate or away from it. The people were promised 200 units of free electricity. They are entitled to ask when that promise will translate into meaningful relief in their monthly household budgets. A government cannot seek political credit for promises and subsequently seek refuge behind regulatory calculations when people demand their implementation. BJP Must Stand With the Consumer The Bharatiya Janata Party should unequivocally stand with the ordinary electricity consumer of Jammu & Kashmir. This is not an issue concerning Jammu or Kashmir alone. A shopkeeper in Jammu, a middle-class employee in Kathua, a farmer in the countryside, a pensioner in Srinagar and a family facing the freezing winter in north or south Kashmir all ultimately confront the same question: How much more can the household budget absorb? The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments. Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months. If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment. Promises Carry a Moral Obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted. An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation. Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so. What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power. The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties. They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them. The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers. Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter. Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers. And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people. Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity. For many families, it is warmth. It is security. It is a basic necessity of life. And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive. (The Author is the Chief Spokesperson of JK BJP)

This means that electricity consumption during the harsh winter months cannot simply be treated as discretionary consumption.
A Kashmiri family using additional electricity to keep its children or elderly parents warm is not indulging in luxury.
It is responding to climatic necessity.
And the timing is particularly unfortunate.
The revised tariff becomes applicable from September 1 and will remain applicable through the approaching winter until March 31, 2027.
The government should therefore ask itself a simple question: Is the period immediately preceding the harsh Kashmir winter the appropriate time to make electricity more expensive for households?
Don't Make Consumers Pay for Inefficiency.
There is undoubtedly a financial problem in the electricity sector.
Power has a cost.
Distribution companies require revenue, and transmission and distribution losses have historically presented a serious challenge.
But the solution cannot perpetually be to transfer the consequences of inefficiency onto honest consumers.

The first responsibility of government should be to reduce losses, improve billing and collection, prevent electricity theft, modernise infrastructure and improve the efficiency of distribution companies.
A family that pays its electricity bill regularly should not become the easiest source for balancing the books.

Before asking consumers to pay more, the government must demonstrate what measurable reduction it has achieved in distribution losses and what administrative reforms it has undertaken to bring down costs.
Efficiency must come before additional burden.
That may constitute an administrative defence.
It does not answer the political question.
The issue is not whether electricity continues to receive subsidy.
The issue is whether the government is moving towards the relief that was promised to the electorate or away from it.
The people were promised 200 units of free electricity.
They are entitled to ask when that promise will translate into meaningful relief in their monthly household budgets.
A government cannot seek political credit for promises and subsequently seek refuge behind regulatory calculations when people demand their implementation.
BJP Must Stand With the Consumer.
The Bharatiya Janata Party should unequivocally stand with the ordinary electricity consumer of Jammu & Kashmir.
This is not an issue concerning Jammu or Kashmir alone.

A shopkeeper in Jammu, a middle-class employee in Kathua, a farmer in the countryside, a pensioner in Srinagar and a family facing the freezing winter in north or south Kashmir all ultimately confront the same question: How much more can the household budget absorb?

The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments.
Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months.

If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment.
Promises Carry a Moral Obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted.
An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation.
Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so.
What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power.
The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties.
They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them.
The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers.
Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter.
Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers.
And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people.
Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity.
For many families, it is warmth.
It is security.
It is a basic necessity of life.
And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive.
(The Author is the Chief Spokesperson of JK BJP).
